The Balkan Wars. Two regional conflicts fought in southeastern Europe between nineteen twelve and nineteen thirteen that dismantled Ottoman territorial holdings and exposed great-power rivalries that would eventually ignite World War One.

The First Balkan War united Serbia, Bulgaria, Greece, and Montenegro against the declining Ottoman Empire. These Balkan nations defeated the Ottomans decisively, forcing them to surrender nearly all their remaining European territories. The Ottomans retained only a small area around Istanbul and the Straits. This outcome revealed Ottoman weakness that had become increasingly apparent throughout the nineteenth century, inviting both local nationalist movements and great-power intervention.

The Second Balkan War erupted just a year later. Bulgaria, dissatisfied with its territorial gains in the First War, attacked its former allies Serbia and Greece in nineteen thirteen. But Bulgaria was defeated and lost additional territory. Serbia emerged as the dominant Balkan Slavic power, strengthening nationalist sentiment and rivaling Austria-Hungary for regional influence and control of Slavic-majority territories.

The great powers competed fiercely for influence in the Balkans. Russia supported the Balkan Slavic nations. Austria-Hungary opposed Serbian expansion, viewing it as a threat to its multi-ethnic empire. Germany backed Austria-Hungary. These tensions transformed the Balkans into a powder keg. The wars exposed the fragility of Ottoman power and the volatility of nationalist aspirations in the region, creating conditions where local conflicts could escalate to world war.

Austria-Hungary's annexation of Bosnia-Herzegovina in nineteen eight and the Balkan Wars reinforced Serbian nationalism and anti-Habsburg sentiment. This resentment culminated in the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in nineteen fourteen, the spark that would ignite the global conflict.

The regional instability and ethnic tensions ignited by the Balkan Wars directly contributed to World War One's outbreak and deeply shaped the conflict's ideological dimensions.
